caption: What if Russia never sold Alaska?
text: What if Russia never sold Alaska?

caption: Russian troops would be guarding the Canadian border. And Soviet missiles would sit on North American soil.
text: Russian troops would be guarding the Canadian border. And Soviet missiles would sit on North American soil.

caption: But in the real world, in 1867, Russia sold it to the United States for just $7.2 million.
text: But in the real world, in eighteen-sixty-seven, Russia sold it to the United States for just seven-point-two million-dollars.

caption: That's more land than Texas, California and Montana combined.
text: That's more land than Texas, California and Montana combined.

caption: So why did Russia sell? And if it hadn't, what would the world look like today? Let's find out.
text: So why did Russia sell? And if it hadn't, what would the world look like today? Let's find out.

caption: First, a geography lesson. Russia and America are neighbors. At its narrowest, the Bering Strait is only about 50 miles wide.
text: First, a geography lesson. Russia and America are neighbors. At its narrowest, the Bering Strait is only about fifty miles wide.

caption: In the middle sit two islands. One is Russian, one is American. They're less than three miles apart.
text: In the middle sit two islands. One is Russian, one is American. They're less than three miles apart.

caption: In 1741, a Danish captain working for the Tsar, Vitus Bering, sailed across and reached the coast of Alaska.
text: In seventeen-forty-one, a Danish captain working for the Tsar, Vitus Bering, sailed across and reached the coast of Alaska.

caption: His crew brought back sea otter pelts. The softest fur in the world, and China paid a fortune for it.
text: His crew brought back sea otter pelts. The softest fur in the world, and China paid a fortune for it.

caption: Word spread fast. Russian fur traders poured across the sea and hunted their way along the Aleutian Islands.
text: Word spread fast. Russian fur traders poured across the sea and hunted their way along the Aleutian Islands.

caption: The people who had lived there for thousands of years, like the Aleut and the Tlingit, were forced to hunt for them, and many times they fought back.
text: The people who had lived there for thousands of years, like the Aleut and the Tlingit, were forced to hunt for them, and many times they fought back.

caption: In 1799, the Tsar created the Russian-American Company, a private monopoly that ran the colony for the state.
text: In seventeen-ninety-nine, the Tsar created the Russian-American Company, a private monopoly that ran the colony for the state.

caption: Its capital was Sitka. Churches, a fort, a shipyard. By the 1830s, more than 1,000 people lived there.
text: Its capital was Sitka. Churches, a fort, a shipyard. By the eighteen-thirties, more than one-thousand people lived there.

caption: Russia even reached California. Fort Ross stood about 90 miles north of San Francisco.
text: Russia even reached California. Fort Ross stood about ninety miles north of San Francisco.

caption: But for all that land, there were never more than about 800 Russians living there.
text: But for all that land, there were never more than about eight-hundred Russians living there.

caption: So why sell? Three reasons.
text: So why sell? Three reasons.

caption: One. The sea otters were almost gone. The money machine was running dry.
text: One. The sea otters were almost gone. The money machine was running dry.

caption: Two. It was too far away. From St. Petersburg, across Siberia, to Alaska could take months.
text: Two. It was too far away. From Saint Petersburg, across Siberia, to Alaska could take months.

caption: And three, the big one. Britain.
text: And three, the big one. Britain.

caption: In 1853, Russia went to war against Britain and France in Crimea. And lost.
text: In eighteen-fifty-three, Russia went to war against Britain and France in Crimea. And lost.

caption: During that war, an Anglo-French fleet sailed all the way to Russia's Pacific port on Kamchatka and attacked it.
text: During that war, an Anglo-French fleet sailed all the way to Russia's Pacific port on Kamchatka and attacked it.

caption: The lesson was clear. In the next war, Britain could march in from Canada and take Alaska, and Russia couldn't stop it.
text: The lesson was clear. In the next war, Britain could march in from Canada and take Alaska, and Russia couldn't stop it.

caption: And Russia was broke after the war. If you're going to lose it anyway, you might as well get paid.
text: And Russia was broke after the war. If you're going to lose it anyway, you might as well get paid.

caption: Sell it to whom? To the enemy of your enemy. The United States, which had its own grudges against Britain.
text: Sell it to whom? To the enemy of your enemy. The United States, which had its own grudges against Britain.

caption: But the deal had to wait. America was busy fighting its own Civil War.
text: But the deal had to wait. America was busy fighting its own Civil War.

caption: When the war ended, one American wanted Alaska badly. Secretary of State William Seward.
text: When the war ended, one American wanted Alaska badly. Secretary of State William Seward.

caption: The Russian minister came to his house one evening. Seward didn't wait for morning. He opened up the State Department that night.
text: The Russian minister came to his house one evening. Seward didn't wait for morning. He opened up the State Department that night.

caption: Before dawn on March 30th, 1867, the treaty was signed.
text: Before dawn on March thirtieth, eighteen-sixty-seven, the treaty was signed.

caption: The price: $7.2 million. About two cents an acre.
text: The price: seven-point-two million-dollars. About two cents an acre.

caption: Critics called it "Seward's Icebox." But here's the thing: most newspapers at the time actually supported the deal.
text: Critics called it Seward's Icebox. But here's the thing: most newspapers at the time actually supported the deal.

caption: Quick quiz. When the Senate voted on the treaty, how many senators voted no? 2, 12, or 20?
text: Quick quiz. When the Senate voted on the treaty, how many senators voted no? Two, twelve, or twenty?

caption: Just 2. It passed 37 to 2.
text: Just two. It passed thirty-seven to two.

caption: On October 18th, 1867, in Sitka, the Russian flag came down and the American flag went up.
text: On October eighteenth, eighteen-sixty-seven, in Sitka, the Russian flag came down and the American flag went up.

caption: Thirty years later, gold was found in the Klondike, and tens of thousands of Americans rushed north through Alaska.
text: Thirty years later, gold was found in the Klondike, and tens of thousands of Americans rushed north through Alaska.

caption: And in 1968, oil at Prudhoe Bay. The biggest oil field in North America. Not a bad return on $7.2 million.
text: And in nineteen-sixty-eight, oil at Prudhoe Bay. The biggest oil field in North America. Not a bad return on seven-point-two million-dollars.

caption: But this deal almost didn't happen. If Seward hadn't been in office, if the Civil War had dragged on, or if the Tsar had changed his mind.
text: But this deal almost didn't happen. If Seward hadn't been in office, if the Civil War had dragged on, or if the Tsar had changed his mind.

caption: So let's go back to 1867, and tear up that treaty.
text: So let's go back to eighteen-sixty-seven, and tear up that treaty.

caption: From here, there are two paths. The most likely one. And the scariest one.
text: From here, there are two paths. The most likely one. And the scariest one.

caption: Path A. Russia's worst fear comes true.
text: Path A. Russia's worst fear comes true.

caption: In that very same year, 1867, Canada was born as a country under the British Crown.
text: In that very same year, eighteen-sixty-seven, Canada was born as a country under the British Crown.

caption: Many historians think that in the next war between Russia and Britain, Alaska would have fallen to the British within a few decades.
text: Many historians think that in the next war between Russia and Britain, Alaska would have fallen to the British within a few decades.

caption: And in the end, Alaska would simply become part of Canada.
text: And in the end, Alaska would simply become part of Canada.

caption: Canada would grow by about a sixth, and it would own both the Klondike gold road and Prudhoe Bay oil.
text: Canada would grow by about a sixth, and it would own both the Klondike gold road and Prudhoe Bay oil.

caption: America would have no Arctic coast at all. And in World War II, there would be no northern route to fly nearly 8,000 warplanes to the Soviets.
text: America would have no Arctic coast at all. And in World War Two, there would be no northern route to fly nearly eight-thousand warplanes to the Soviets.

caption: In the real world, Japan seized the Alaskan islands of Attu and Kiska in 1942. In Path A, that's Canada's fight.
text: In the real world, Japan seized the Alaskan islands of Attu and Kiska in nineteen-forty-two. In Path A, that's Canada's fight.

caption: Path A sounds quiet. But it changes one thing forever. America would no longer be Russia's neighbor.
text: Path A sounds quiet. But it changes one thing forever. America would no longer be Russia's neighbor.

caption: Path B. Britain never comes, and Russia hangs on to Alaska, all the way to 1917.
text: Path B. Britain never comes, and Russia hangs on to Alaska, all the way to nineteen-seventeen.

caption: That year, revolution. The Tsar is overthrown, and a civil war follows.
text: That year, revolution. The Tsar is overthrown, and a civil war follows.

caption: In the real world, America actually sent about 8,000 troops into Siberia, landing at Vladivostok.
text: In the real world, America actually sent about eight-thousand troops into Siberia, landing at Vladivostok.

caption: In Path B, America might grab Alaska in the chaos. But let's say it fails, and the Reds win.
text: In Path B, America might grab Alaska in the chaos. But let's say it fails, and the Reds win.

caption: Now the Soviet Union owns a piece of North America, with a land border to Canada over 1,500 miles long.
text: Now the Soviet Union owns a piece of North America, with a land border to Canada over one-thousand-five-hundred miles long.

caption: In 1962, the Soviets put missiles in Cuba, 90 miles from Florida, and the world came close to nuclear war.
text: In nineteen-sixty-two, the Soviets put missiles in Cuba, ninety miles from Florida, and the world came close to nuclear war.

caption: In Path B, there's nothing to smuggle. The missiles are already on Soviet soil, less than 1,000 miles from Seattle.
text: In Path B, there's nothing to smuggle. The missiles are already on Soviet soil, less than one-thousand miles from Seattle.

caption: Prudhoe Bay oil would pay for the Red Army, not for America.
text: Prudhoe Bay oil would pay for the Red Army, not for America.

caption: And Canada becomes the front line of the Cold War, like West Germany in our world.
text: And Canada becomes the front line of the Cold War, like West Germany in our world.

caption: America would have to pour its troops and money into defending its own continent.
text: America would have to pour its troops and money into defending its own continent.

caption: So what would that mean for you?
text: So what would that mean for you?

caption: At its peak in 1988, Alaska's North Slope pumped about a quarter of all the oil produced in the United States.
text: At its peak in nineteen-eighty-eight, Alaska's North Slope pumped about a quarter of all the oil produced in the United States.

caption: Since 1982, every Alaskan has received a yearly check from that oil money. The Permanent Fund Dividend.
text: Since nineteen-eighty-two, every Alaskan has received a yearly check from that oil money. The Permanent Fund Dividend.

caption: About six out of every ten pounds of wild seafood caught in the US comes from Alaskan waters.
text: About six out of every ten pounds of wild seafood caught in the US comes from Alaskan waters.

caption: And today, most of America's long-range missile interceptors are based in Alaska, at Fort Greely, guarding the whole country.
text: And today, most of America's long-range missile interceptors are based in Alaska, at Fort Greely, guarding the whole country.

caption: In Path B, every one of those flips. The oil, the fish, the shield. Instead of protecting you, that land would be aimed at you.
text: In Path B, every one of those flips. The oil, the fish, the shield. Instead of protecting you, that land would be aimed at you.

caption: Back to the real world.
text: Back to the real world.

caption: Russia sold because it knew it couldn't keep Alaska. Better to get paid than lose it to Britain for nothing. At the time, it made sense.
text: Russia sold because it knew it couldn't keep Alaska. Better to get paid than lose it to Britain for nothing. At the time, it made sense.

caption: America got more than gold and oil. It got a front door to the Pacific and the Arctic.
text: America got more than gold and oil. It got a front door to the Pacific and the Arctic.

caption: And without the deal, the likely ending is a Canadian Alaska. The scary one is the Soviets in North America.
text: And without the deal, the likely ending is a Canadian Alaska. The scary one is the Soviets in North America.

caption: So, if you were the Tsar in 1867, would you have sold? Tell me in the comments.
text: So, if you were the Tsar in eighteen-sixty-seven, would you have sold? Tell me in the comments.

text: Next time: what if Napoleon never sold Louisiana, and half of America stayed French?
